beads.title: An MDM policy file is parsed, typed and reported, and then applied to nothing
beads.description: Go applies the effective policy to prefs in `applySysPolicyLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) and keeps re-applying it: `registerSysPolicyWatch` runs it once at startup and registers a change callback, `sysPolicyChanged` -> `reconcilePrefs` re-runs it whenever a setting moves, and a profile load goes through the same reconcile. What it applies is specific. `LoginURL` overrides `Prefs.ControlURL`. `Hostname` overrides the hostname, or -- when the key is present but empty -- CLEARS it, a tri-state Go implements with a `"HostnameDefaultValue"` sentinel precisely because "not configured" and "configured to empty" have to mean opposite things. `applyExitNodeSysPolicyLocked` pins `ExitNodeID` or `ExitNodeIP` (mutually exclusive: setting the ID clears the IP), parses an `auto:`-prefixed value as an `ExitNodeExpression`, and for as long as that expression is unresolved parks `ExitNodeID` on a deliberately invalid id so traffic blackholes rather than leaking outside the policy while the pick is being made. `AlwaysOn.Enabled` forces `WantRunning` back to true unless a valid user override stands. And eight `preferencePolicies` entries map a `PreferenceOption` key onto one bool pref each: `AllowIncomingConnections` (the negation of shields-up), `UnattendedMode`, `ExitNodeAllowLANAccess`, `UseTailscaleDNSSettings`, `UseTailscaleSubnets`, `CheckUpdates`, `InstallUpdates` and `AdvertiseExitNode`. This fork has the whole left-hand side of that and none of the right. `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` is a faithful port of Go's RESOLUTION: it defines every one of those keys with its Go value type, merges sources last-writer-wins, and reports the snapshot with per-key origin and error -- and its own module doc states the gap outright ("The snapshot is *reported* (`tnet syspolicy list`/`reload`); it is not yet *applied* to prefs."). The only consumers anywhere in the daemon are `tailnetd`'s two by-name reads, `EncryptState` and `HardwareAttestation`, which power two startup refusals of their own. So an administrator can ship a policy file, run `tnet syspolicy list`, watch `Hostname`, `ExitNodeID` and `AllowIncomingConnections` echoed back with their origin, and find the node completely unchanged -- which is worse than having no policy support at all, because a report that renders the admin's intent looks exactly like enforcement of it. Three decisions before porting. WHICH keys: the eight preference options plus `LoginURL` and `Hostname` are mechanical (each is one pref this fork already models), but `ExitNodeID`/`ExitNodeIP` land on the exit-node selector model this fork just built (`resolve_exit_node_arg` in src/ipn/mod.rs) and on the `auto:` expression it deliberately refuses by name, so the blackhole-id behaviour needs its own ruling rather than a transcription. WHERE it runs: Go reconciles on profile load and on every policy change, and this fork's only source is a JSON file read once at startup, so the honest MVP applies at load and again on `syspolicy reload`, and says so where the source is documented. PRECEDENCE: policy must beat a live `tnet set`, which is the entire point of policy, so its interaction with the accidental-revert guard (src/ipn/revert_guard.rs) and with `--config`'s `Locked` rule has to be decided in the open rather than discovered by whoever hits it first.

beads.title: --operator is persisted and handed to the engine, and grants its user nothing
beads.description: Go's LocalAPI write gate is `ConnIdentity.IsReadonlyConn` (ipn/ipnauth/ipnauth.go), a five-arm decision evaluated per connection and logged at every arm so an operator can see which rule decided: peer uid 0 gets write ("root has access"); a non-root daemon whose own uid equals the peer's gets write; THE UID NAMED BY `Prefs.OperatorUser` gets write ("is configured operator"); a local admin gets write (`isLocalAdmin` -- a member of group `admin` on darwin, `administrators` on QNAP, and an explicit "no system admin group found" error anywhere else); everyone else is read-only. `ipnserver.actor.Permissions` (ipn/ipnserver/server.go) turns that into the `PermitRead`/`PermitWrite` pair the LocalAPI handlers consult, and `userIDFromString` resolves the pref's value as either a username or a numeric uid before the comparison. The pref is upstream's documented escape from sudo: when a LocalAPI call is denied, `cmd/tailscale/cli/cli.go` appends "To not require root, use 'sudo tailscale set --operator=$USER' once." to the error. This fork implements arms one and two and stops. `AuthPolicy::access_for_uid` (src/auth.rs) grants `ReadWrite` to uid 0 or the daemon's euid and `ReadOnly` to everyone else, and the module doc calls the operator tier "a later phase", naming `AuthPolicy` plus the peer gid as the seam for it. `Prefs::operator_user` (src/prefs.rs) persists the value, `src/ipn/config.rs` threads it into the engine `Config`, and its rustdoc says plainly that setting it today "neither widens nor narrows who may drive the daemon". So the single command Go's own error text tells a user to run is inert here, and this daemon's refusal ("permission denied: writing (up/down) requires root or the same user that owns the daemon", src/server.rs) does not mention the pref that is supposed to fix it. Decide the scope deliberately, because unlike most rows in this backlog this one WIDENS access rather than narrowing it. The operator arm is the ask: resolve `operator_user` to a uid -- Go accepts a name or a number -- and consult it in `access_for_uid`, with the name resolution done where the pref is SET so a username that resolves to nothing is refused at `set` time instead of silently denying forever. The local-admin arm is a separate ruling: on macOS it grants write to every member of the `admin` group, which is most desktop accounts on the platform this daemon builds and runs on, while docs/THREAT_MODEL.md section 4.1 currently promises a peer-uid gate. Port it or decline it in writing; silence is what makes the next sweep re-find it. Note this is not `tsd-euv`: that bead moves the LocalAPI from newline-JSON to Go's HTTP/1-over-UDS transport and would carry `PermitRead`/`PermitWrite` as a wire concern, where this is about who those two bits are computed for.

beads.title: down --reason satisfies no policy, because always-on mode is not enforced
beads.description: `ipnauth.CheckDisconnectPolicy` (ipn/ipnauth/policy.go) is the rule `--reason` exists to satisfy, and it is three refusals in one function. With `AlwaysOn.Enabled` unset it returns nil and anyone may disconnect. With it set and `AlwaysOn.OverrideWithReason` unset, a disconnect is refused outright: "disconnect not allowed: always-on mode is enabled". With both set, an empty reason is refused -- "disconnect not allowed: reason required" -- and a non-empty one is accepted AND written to the audit log as `tailcfg.AuditNodeDisconnect`, with the actor's username when the platform has one. The reason travels from the CLI as `apitype.RequestReasonKey` on the prefs edit, which is exactly the shape this fork already carries. Around that rule sit two more pieces of the same mechanism: `onEditPrefsLocked` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) records `overrideAlwaysOn` when a permitted disconnect happens and arms the `ReconnectAfter` timer that brings the node back up on its own, and `applySysPolicyLocked` forces `WantRunning` true again for as long as no override stands -- so always-on is not a single check but a loop, and `Start`, a profile switch and any change to the two AlwaysOn keys all reset the override. This fork has both inputs and neither rule. `Request::Down` and `Request::Logout` (src/localapi.rs) carry an `Option<String>` reason, `src/server.rs` sanitizes it for the daemon log and records it alongside the disconnect, and the localapi rustdoc admits the scope: "in Go the reason is what lets a user disconnect a node whose MDM policy" would otherwise refuse. `src/ipn/syspolicy.rs` already defines and types all three keys -- `AlwaysOn.Enabled`, `AlwaysOn.OverrideWithReason` and `ReconnectAfter` (as a Go duration). So `tnet down` on a policy- managed node succeeds, the reason is written to a log nobody audits, and the administrator's always-on setting does nothing. Decide the boundary and the depth. The refusals belong in the daemon, at the one place `WantRunning` goes from true to false, so `down`, `logout` and a LocalAPI prefs edit share them; `tnet` may refuse earlier for a better message but must not be the only gate. The depth decision is `ReconnectAfter`: the refusals alone are a day's work and are the part with operator- visible value, while the reconnect timer is a background task with its own lifecycle questions (what cancels it, what happens across a daemon restart) and can be a follow-up -- but say which was taken. This is NOT engine ask #41: that ask is the reason REACHING CONTROL as a client audit log, which needs an engine transport this daemon does not have. The refusal half is local, needs nothing from the engine, and is what actually stops the disconnect.

beads.title: A Go command line that omits the tag: prefix is refused, where Go completes it
beads.description: `prefsFromUpArgs` (cmd/tailscale/cli/up.go) splits `--advertise-tags` on commas and then does one thing to each value before validating it, with the reason in the comment: "Allow users to omit the `tag:` prefix; if the tag has no colon at all, add it for them." So `--advertise-tags server,ci` is rewritten to `tag:server,tag:ci` and accepted. A value that DOES contain a colon is passed through untouched, which is what makes `--advertise-tags foo:bar` fail with "tags must start with 'tag:'" rather than quietly becoming `tag:foo:bar`. Only after that rewrite does `tailcfg.CheckTag` run: cut the `tag:` prefix, refuse an empty name, refuse a name whose first byte is not a letter, refuse any byte that is not a letter, digit or `-`. Go then reports a failure as `tag: %q: %s` with the REWRITTEN value quoted, so the operator sees the tag as the daemon would have seen it. This fork ports `CheckTag` and skips the rewrite. `validate_advertise_tags` (src/ipn/mod.rs) requires the prefix outright -- `strip_prefix("tag:")` or "invalid tag {t:?}: tags must be of the form tag:<name> (e.g. tag:server)" -- and it runs daemon-side on both the `up` and the `set` path, with nothing in `tnet` touching the values on the way: src/bin/tnet.rs's own comment records that "any value VALIDATION -- CIDR parsing for routes, `tag:` form for tags -- happens elsewhere". So `tnet up --advertise-tags server` is refused where `tailscale up --advertise-tags server` succeeds, and it is refused by a rule an operator copying upstream's documentation has no reason to expect. Decide where the rewrite lives, and keep the two halves apart. Go rewrites and validates in the CLI; this fork validates in the daemon precisely so `up` and `set` share ONE rule, which argues for rewriting there too rather than growing a second, CLI-side notion of what a tag is. The alternative -- rewrite in `tnet`, leave the daemon strict -- keeps the LocalAPI's contract unambiguous (`tag:<name>` or nothing) at the cost of the completion being a CLI courtesy a direct LocalAPI caller does not get; Go's own split is exactly that, so it is defensible, but say which was taken. The colon rule is the part to port exactly: completion applies only when the value contains NO colon at all, so a malformed `foo:bar` still reaches `CheckTag` and is refused by name instead of being turned into a tag nobody asked for. Worth aligning the message shape while in there, since Go quotes the completed value and this fork quotes the value as typed.

beads.title: A lone default route is advertised happily, where Go demands its other-family counterpart
beads.description: `netutil.CalcAdvertiseRoutes` (net/netutil/routes.go) is the one place Go turns `--advertise-routes` plus `--advertise-exit-node` into a route SET, and three of its rules have no counterpart in this fork. (1) A default route advertised in one family only is refused: if `0.0.0.0/0` is present and `::/0` is not, "0.0.0.0/0 advertised without its IPv6 counterpart, please also advertise ::/0", and the mirror message for the reverse. That is the rule that stops a half-working exit node -- a node advertising only the v4 default takes v4 traffic from clients that then send v6 straight out their own link, which is a traffic leak an operator has no way to see from either end. (2) A 4via6 prefix is validated by `ValidateViaPrefix`: inside the Tailscale via range, a prefix length of at least /96, and an embedded site id no greater than 0xffff, each with its own message. (3) The set is de-duplicated and sorted, and `--advertise-exit-node` is folded in as the two default routes rather than carried as a separate flag, which is why Go's `AdvertisesExitNode()` is a question about the route set and not about a bool. This fork has some of the pieces and runs none of them on an advertised route: `tnet debug via` (src/bin/tnet.rs) already encodes and decodes 4via6 routes and already enforces Go's "at least a /96" rule there, and nothing applies it to `--advertise-routes`. The prefs path validates routes one at a time and never as a set. `Backend::check_prefs_gated` (src/ipn/mod.rs) parses each entry as `ipnet::IpNet` and checks only that it equals its masked form ("route %s has non-address bits set; expected %s"), the up/set path re-parses the same way before persisting, and `src/conffile.rs` does the identical per-route check for `AdvertiseRoutes` from a config file. So `tnet up --advertise-routes 0.0.0.0/0` is accepted, advertises half an exit node, and nothing anywhere says so; a malformed 4via6 prefix is accepted and advertised as an ordinary route. Decide two things. First, whether to keep `advertise_exit_node` as a separate pref or fold it into the route set the way Go does: this fork models it separately and `check_prefs` already refuses the advertise-and-use conflict on that basis, so the pairing rule has to be evaluated against the routes the two inputs produce TOGETHER, not against the flag's literal argument. Second, where it lands: the rule is a property of the final route set, so it belongs beside the existing masking check in the shared prefs validation, which puts it on `up`, `set`, `check-prefs` and the config loader at once -- and the config loader is the path that most needs it, since a declaratively-managed subnet router is exactly the deployment where nobody is watching the command output.

beads.title: A launchd-managed daemon has no file in which to set the envknobs it now obeys
beads.description: `envknob.ApplyDiskConfig` (envknob/envknob.go) runs at the top of Go's `tailscaled` `main`, before a single flag is registered: it reads a `tailscaled-env.txt` of `KEY=value` lines and applies them to the daemon's own environment. `getPlatformEnvFiles` picks the path per platform -- `%ProgramData%\Tailscale\tailscaled-env.txt` on Windows; on darwin, the sandboxed GUI builds look beside `$HOME` and the working directory, while a non-sandboxed `tailscaled`-on-macOS (the homebrew shape this fork ships a formula for) reads `/etc/tailscale/tailscaled-env.txt`; on ordinary Linux it is deliberately nothing, because `/etc/default/tailscaled` already does the job through the service manager. `applyKeyValueEnv` is small and exactly specified: trim, skip blank lines and `#` comments, cut at the first `=`, trim both halves, `strconv.Unquote` a value that starts with a double quote, refuse the file with "invalid value in line %q" if that unquote fails, and `Setenv` the rest. A failure is stashed in `applyDiskConfigErr` and surfaced by `ApplyDiskConfigError()` for the health tracker, so a typo in an administrator's env file becomes a health warning rather than silence. This fork reads administrative envknobs and gives macOS no way to set them. The systemd unit it installs carries the Linux equivalent (`EnvironmentFile=-/etc/default/tailnetd`, with the optional `-` prefix so an absent file does not fail the unit -- src/ipn/install.rs), and its launchd plist (packaging/launchd/cloud.tailscaled-rs.tailnetd.plist) carries an `EnvironmentVariables` dict with two hardcoded keys, `TS_RS_EXPERIMENT` and `TAILNETD_STATE_DIR` -- but that plist is embedded in the binary with `include_str!` and written out by `tnet install`, so an operator's addition to the dict is lost on the next install. There is no file the daemon reads that the installer does not own. The knobs are no longer hypothetical: `TS_DISABLE_SSH_SERVER` (src/featureknob.rs) is now the operator's off switch for the SSH server and `TS_DISABLE_PORTMAPPER` (src/portmap.rs) for the port mapper. Both are read at the moment the daemon decides, and on a launchd-managed macOS host there is no supported place to put either one. Decide the path and the breadth. Go's macOS path is `/etc/tailscale/tailscaled-env.txt`, which this fork should not borrow verbatim -- it is another project's directory, and this daemon already names its Linux seam `/etc/default/tailnetd`, so the obvious choice is `/etc/tailnetd/tailnetd-env.txt` or similar, chosen once and documented where the launchd unit is. Port the parser as Go states it, including the unquote refusal, because an env file that half-applies is worse than one that is rejected. And decide whether the parse error becomes a health warning now or waits for the health tracker: the warnable is already named in the parity ledger's health row, but nothing populates it, so the honest interim is to refuse at startup with the line number rather than to stash an error nothing will ever read.
